translations.translation: With the help of Heaven.
Shabbos Parshas Korach,
3 Tammuz 5718*

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: Explains that the life in which G-d placed our soul is above nature, preventing our foot from stumbling.

translations.translation: "Hashem placed our soul in life, and did not give our foot to stumbling"1,
and it is explained by my revered father-in-law, the Rebbe, in his maamar beginning with the words "Zeh" of the Festival of Redemption, 12 Tammuz2
[that the beginning of the redemption was on 3 Tammuz3],
that the life in which He placed our soul are levels of life higher than the life of the soul
(in and of itself).
For the life of the soul is limited,
for although the soul is inherently alive
(above the diffusion of vitality that enlivens the body,
and not only particular vitality but also general vitality)4,
nevertheless,
since this that the soul is inherently alive is because the Holy One, blessed be He, implanted in the soul this nature
(that it should be inherently alive),
therefore,
even this vitality
(of the aspect of being inherently alive)
is within limitation,
and the life in which He placed our soul is above nature5.
And this is "Hashem placed our soul in life, and did not give our foot to stumbling,"
that the power for our feet not to stumble comes specifically from the life that is above nature.

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: Introduces the need to understand why the soul's own life can lead to stumbling, and connects this to the dispute of Korach and the firmament that separates.

translations.translation: And to understand the reason for this, that from the perspective of the life of the soul itself,
even from the aspect of being inherently alive,
it is possible for our foot to stumble,
and the power for our foot not to stumble comes specifically from the life that is above nature,
and also to understand the connection of this matter to the redemption of 12 Tammuz,
we must preface what is stated at the beginning of our parshah6:
"And Korach took," and Onkelos translated: "And Korach separated."
For wherever it says "vayikach" he translated "vensav," but here he translated "vesapleg."
And it is brought in the sefer Noam Elimelech7
that "vesapleg"
(Korach)
is like the firmament that separates between water and water.
And the Tzemach Tzedek explains8,
that this interpretation
(that "vesapleg Korach" is like the firmament that separates)
is based on what is brought in the Zohar9,
that the firmament that separates was a dispute of left with right, etc., like the dispute of Korach with Aharon.
From this it is understood,
that the connection of "vesapleg Korach" to the firmament that separates is not only because the root of dispute
(any dispute whatsoever)
is from the firmament that separates,
as it is brought in the Midrash10:
Why is "ki tov" not written on the second day? Because on it dispute was created, as it is said11,
"And it separated between water and water,"
but rather, even this particular dispute,
the dispute of Korach with Aharon,
is analogous to
(and its root is)
the dispute of the firmament that separates.
For just as the dispute of the firmament that separates is a dispute of left with right,
so too is the dispute of Korach with Aharon,
for Aharon is in the line of Chessed,
right,
and Korach, who was a Levite, was from the aspect of Gevuros,
left.
